/Issued 232 PM MST Tue Nov 24 2026/ 

 - Meteorological Overview:

Transient ridging passes through the Northern Rockies tonight for
continued moderating temperatures and breezy to windy conditions 
along the Rocky Mountain Front and the plains. There were some 
drifting snow issues earlier this morning, but this concern has 
largely been abated with temperatures rising above freezing. 
Lighter winds and inversions will maintain cooler conditions for 
southwest MT, especially the wind protected valleys where low 
clouds and dense fog patches may develop again tonight depending 
on how fast mid- and higher level clouds move in tonight.

A shortwave quickly displaces the ridge on Wednesday, although 
this will do little more than continue to increase mid- and higher
level clouds and perhaps bring a few spotty rain/snow showers 
along the northern divide. Westerly flow increases markedly 
Wednesday night through Friday in response to a Pacific trough 
moving atop a ridge centered over the Great Basin and southwestern
CONUS. H700/H500 winds increase to around 2 to 3 standard 
deviations above climatology and peak in strength late Thursday 
into early Friday. This combined with mountain wave activity will 
transfer strong winds to the surface along the Rocky Mountain 
Front and nearby high plains. Pacific moisture will also begin 
streaming into the Northern Rockies and initially bring mountain 
snow to areas along the Continental Divide. 

Another trough then quickly dives southeastward and ushers in a 
more northwesterly flow aloft Friday into Saturday. This will slow
the winds down a bit and expand the snow eastward to the central 
and southwestern mountains. As the jet stream sags southward, H700
temperatures will cool down to the -.5 to -10C range and bring at
least some snow to lower elevations by Saturday; however, 
appreciable accumulations will mostly be confined to the 
northwesterly facing foothills of the central and southwest 
mountains. The overall unsettled zonal flow will persist into next
week with temperatures looking to remain near or slightly below 
average. - RCG

 - Forecast Confidence & Scenarios:

Gusty to strong winds late Thursday through early Friday...

Model guidance supports the strongest winds coinciding with the 
arrival of a vigorous Pacific trough Thursday into Thursday night.
Initially the 50 kt + H700 winds look to be confined to the Rocky
Mountain Front before broadening and expanding deeper into the 
plains Thursday evening. With the strongest and most widespread 
winds aloft generally occurring after sunset, there will be a 
heavier reliance on mountain wave activity to achieve 55+ mph wind
gusts over the plains, and this would mostly favor the eastern 
Glacier /western Toole County zone in the late afternoon and early
evening hours followed by the central MT highway 87/200 corridor 
later in the evening and overnight hours, especially Judith Basin 
County. NBM probabilities support westerly winds gusting over 60 
mph regularly along the Rocky Mountain Front and plains along and 
west of highway 89 during this time, along with a 40 to 60% chance
for gusts over 75 mph. 

Farther east, the Cut Bank area is still the most favorable area 
for gusts exceeding 60 mph based on forecast soundings/previous 
analogs followed by the lower elevation of Judith Basin County. 
Impacts will be greatest for those traveling with high profile 
vehicles or towing light weight trailers, especially along highway
89 north of the Choteau Junction. 

There is a small chance that the stronger winds will break the 
crust of snowpack along the immediate eastern slopes of the Rocky 
Mountain Front, resulting in blowing and drifting snow; however, 
warming temperatures and the shrinking snow base has decreased 
this risk to less than 20%. No changes were made to the inherited 
high wind watches other than extending them through 8 AM Friday to
cover winds looking to be slower to shut down Friday morning. 
Some consideration was given to expand the watch to include 
portions of the central MT highway 87/200, but held off for now 
due to lack of confidence in robust mountain waves. 

Mostly mountain snow Thursday through the weekend...

A Pacific trough crosses the Continental Divide on Thursday and 
increases PWATS to around 2 standard deviations above climatology.
Downsloping will initially confine accumulating snow to areas 
along and immediately east of the divide; however, another trough 
deepens and brings colder air aloft Friday into Saturday for more 
expansive mountain snow, with snow levels dropping to the 
valley’s/plain’s floor by Saturday morning. About 40% of the 
ensembles support accumulating snow generally in the 2 to 7 inch 
range for the higher terrain along the Continental Divide and over
the central/southwestern mountain ranges. The highest amounts 
look to be over the Madison and Gallatin ranges. Lower elevations
